Mr. SOLON E. LOW (Peace River): Mr. Speaker, on a question of personal privilege, I have before me the Ottawa Journal of Wednesday, August 7. On page 3 is an article entitled, "Low charges Mr. King courted communists." The heading and the body of the article are both inaccurate in reporting the contents of my speech at Noranda, Quebec, on the evening of August 5. I wish to ask a question in regard to these securities. For the benefit
(Mr. Church.]
of the hon. member for Halton, I had not thought of this question when the committee was holding its meetings. Apparently no one is allowed to take securities with him should he change his residence to the United States. Let us suppose that an elderly person has arthritis or some other difficulty and goes to a warmer climate. Naturally he wants to remove the means by which he lives. Suppose that particular Canadian had the foresight to provide himself in Canada with United States securities, as is easily done under the present regulations of the board, as follows, namely, by selling Canadian securities which are saleable in New York and obtaining funds and putting these United States funds into United States securities. I understand that a Canadian going to the United States will not be declared a resident of that country under the interpretation section of the -bill except within the discretion of the board itself. Does it matter to the board whether that man is allowed to take with him the United States securities which he has purchased while here in Canada from the proceeds of sales 'of Canadian securities in New York? When the witness was before the committee the suggestion was made that there was a certain pool of United States funds which was available to the Canadian economy through the sale of Canadian securities to United States citizens. What I am suggesting to the minister is that there is a pool of United States money at a certain time in exchange for Canadian securities; but if that pool is not dipped into at the particular time it is gone, lost forever, and then you must wait until some Americans want to buy some more Canadian securities. I do not understand how the Canadian economy can be in any way damaged or this right to acquire more United States funds lessened by reason of the fact that the Canadian who was about to settle in the United States provided himself with United States funds at a particular time and then, when he established residence over there, he wished to take those funds with him. How can the board possibly have its scope so far as United States funds are concerned lessened by the transaction which I have just outlined?

were allowed to go over the border and get their money and bring it home. Any man who was well known, a prominent citizen, could go to a bank and get sixteen, eighteen or twenty per cent. If I went in, dressed roughly, and perhaps with fish scales in my hair I would not get the same theatment. I know of many cases of that kind. I remember the case of a man who came with his wife to the town where I lived, and I may say before going farther that as a rule the larger the amount of money you had, the greater percentage you received. This man's wife had 81,000 to deposit in the Bank of Nova Scotia in St. Andrews, and incidentally, I may say, the manager of that bank is still living. She deposited her money and received twelve per cent. Her husband came with S700 and when he deposited his amount he received eighteen per cent. As they were about to leave for home he mentioned to his wife that he had got eighteen per cent and she was surprised to hear that. Although the bank was closed by that time, they went back and the manager discovered that he had made a mistake and the other six per cent was paid.
I do not know what conditions were like in the larger centres, but I know that in New Brunswick the rate of exchange was never at any time posted in the banks. I know of another case-this gentleman is living to-day. At that time he lived in the town of St. George, and it is interesting to know that there are many "saints" in Charlotte county. He had a certain amount of money to deposit and at one bank he was offered twelve per cent. He came to St. Andrews and they offered him fifteen per cent. Then he went to the Bank of Montreal in St. Stephen and was offered twenty per cent-all on the same day.
My chief reason for supporting this measure is that the foreign exchange control situation has been so handled during the war years that every man in the country, regardless of whether he wore a top hat or, as I have said, had fish scales in his hair, got the same treatment when he went to the bank. Everybody got ten per cent. That is the fair and just way of handling the situation, and I have no doubt whatever that if to-day the foreign exchange control board were thrown aside the same thing would happen as happened during the period of which I have spoken. You would find shysters on both sides buying and selling exchange. That happened before and I have no doubt it would happen again.
One hon. member to-night suggested that these regulations were going to create a nation of law-breakers. I suggest that if 63260-285J
we dispensed with the foreign exchange control that we have had during the war we would have a nation of lawbreakers, and they would be the banks and bankers. In my opinion we should stick to the board and allow them to carry on as they have been doing in the past five or six years.

There is no doubt that we had a good many valuable officials in connection with the foreign exchange control board in war time. They did good work during the war. I suggest, however, that there is too much red tape about the regulations. These controls remind me of the game called winding and unwinding, in which the players rehearse a large' number of words and repeat them backwards. In my opinion we are surrendering too much of our financial initiative to Washington all along. We have had controls of foreign currency for five or six years and, if we are to wait for another eighteen months or two years before these controls are all removed, our businessmen will be hamstrung. We have nothing but officials, filing clerks and all the rest of it from the cradle to the grave over exports and foreign exchange, and no business, large or small, can possibly carry on under the interpretation definitions in this section.
Industry and labour in Canada worked wonders in the war and they can work wonders again in peace, but the prime necessity is stability in the delivery of all classes of consumer goods so as to promote our peacetime economy and provide the fullest measure of employment and export of goods and services. But how are our businessmen to do this under these definitions as set out under (a) and (b) as to property and sale by residents of "goods" to be exported. Under this control system we shall have to maintain a whole staff of employees of the foreign exchange control board. As I say, there is altogether too much red tape about the regulations, with armies of officials who think we cannot now live without them.
I have seen the way in which these regulations work at Fort Erie. I come from a commercial city in which there is a heavy American trade by water and rail. I have seen goods coming in and export of goods to nonresidents, and I know the difficulties which businessmen, large and small, have to put up with to meet market demands. I fail to see why, fifteen months after the war, we should continue to maintain these irksome controls, which interfere with the freedom of our people. Various transactions which were not regarded as offences in time of peace were created offences during the war; but the war years

I should like to draw to the attention of the minister a condition which, somewhere between the foreign exchange control board and the Minister of Trade and Commerce, is proving a hardship. I speak on behalf of citizens of the upper St. Lawrence, Wolfe island and Howe island, which I represented in the upper house for fifteen years, and I want to endorse everything that was said by the hon. member for Stanstead. These farmers who have been living in the vicinity of Howe island and Wolfe island have been going back and forth across the border; in fact they are nearer to the United States border than they are to their own county town. Strawberry producers were practically put out of business two or three years ago on account of these controls. But I want to refer particularly to a man in my own city who went over to Saratoga Springs with a string of horses. He tried to get a permit to take a few oats over to the United States, and this was refused.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I do not want to interrupt my hon. friend, but this has nothing to do with the foreign exchange control board.

But there is an overlapping. I wish the Minister of Trade and Commerce was in his seat at the present time. As I said, here was a man with a string of horses going to the United States, and he cannot get oats for them and cannot bring oats in. The results are obvious.
Feed them hay.

You cannot even get hay over there. We have at Kingston one of the finest racetracks there is; northern New York has nothing to touch it. Men arrange to take six or eight horses over, and then they are turned down at the border when they want to take over a few bags of oats. It is a nuisance, and I think that between the Acting Minister of Finance, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and some of their officials it should be possible to issue a permit to a horseman allowing him to take eight or ten or a dozen bags of oats in the back of his truck to feed his horses over there.

I want to put a question that will not be as noisy as some of the questions that have been asked. To-day there is a large export trade growing up, that is large in number, to what are called the free port zones in New York. These zones are especially established for dutiable goods. I am wondering whether we shall have any protection under this new bill and these export regulations. To-day an exporter has, we will say, a thousand dollars worth of dutiable goods going into the United States. He just ships that with an ordinary permit, or has been shipping it with an ordinary permit. He does not have to declare any valuation except for insurance. Those goods, if they are shipped to New York, are shipped to the New York free port zone. The goods are not in bond but they are dutiable. The exporter ships through some chartered bank which has an agency there. Then the exporter notifies the man to whom he expects to sell, and that man goes to the free port zone and examines the goods. A price is then placed on them -by the exporter which is sufficient to cover the value, plus the exporter's profit, -plus the duty that will be paid on the goods. The buyer has nothing to do with the duty. He just goes in and looks at these goods and, if they are worth to him the price which the exporter states, he buys them. He pays -the bank, and the bank pays the United States customs officer the duty. What I want to know is, when that transaction is completed, how the funds will be handled and how the exporter will be protected under this new bill.

statistics on wheat and other things produced in Canada. Those were very satisfactoiy. That branch had many able men, and I do not see why there is so much duplication and triplication of bureaucracy in the form of various boards, commissions, branches, bureaus, et cetera.

Do you remember his name? Was it Gulliver?

I know very well, but I wanted my hon. friend to show how well read he is. It was a classic. When as a child I read "Gulliver's Travels" by Swift, if I am not mistaken, I was enchanted. But I said to myself, how can a giant be tied up by dwarfs like that? I never thought I would see it done in the year 1946, that I would be a member of parliament then and actually see it done here in the House of Commons. We have through this board of duplication of services for which the taxpayer has to pay. I admit that hon. gentlemen have a right to lay their grievances against the board before this committee. I will go farther and say that it is their duty to do so. But on the other hand, if we want to stop these grievances against the board for good, we have simply to give no power to the foreign exchange control board, and I ask the committee not to forget what I said yesterday, that the only way to reform that board is to abolish it. It is the fifth wheel of the coach of state.

tions of the bill in relation to imports and exports, sections 25 and 26. WThat information can we get from this board about the shipment of various products since the beginning of the war? What about the shipment of cheese? What about the shipment of powdered milk? What about the shipment of meat, dressed meat, frozen meat and canned meat? What about the shipment of wheat and other grains? In the Department of Trade and Commerce we have gentlemen who are most serviceable to members of parliament. We have to go to them sometimes when we are sending gifts to another country to find out if they are dutiable in that country, and they give us that information. What information can one get from the foreign exchange control board? What is the personnel of that board? What is the personnel that looks after imports? What is the personnel that looks after exports? I do not understand how any gentleman can complain about bureaucracy if he does not seize this unique opportunity to redress wrongs, to put a stop to them, and at the same time make life easier for the businessman, who at the present time has to go to the board and get this permit and that permit, then come back and get another permit, then have it countersigned by one expert, and even that counter-signature is not enough but must be initialed by another super brain. Foreign Exchange Control

I have in mind the case of a farmer who exported two cords of wood. When he came to the border he was asked to fill out the B form which the minister has spoken about, indicating how much he expected to receive for the wood. He said he had sold the wood for $30, and he made out the B form, stating that he would return $30 and sell it to the bank. The bank was acting as the agent for the foreign exchange control board. The man overlooked the fact that when he was in Maine he would have to spend $1 for his dinner. When he came back he had only $29, and he had to write a number of letters and the banker had to write a number of letters to the foreign exchange control board explaining why it was that he had not brought back $30.

Inasmuch as our dollar is now on a parity with the United States dollar, does not the reason for this provision in the bill, within the limits of the amendment, pretty well disappear? When there was a difference of ten per cent it was a much more serious matter than it is now. Another regulation imposed on the small exporter means an additional deterrent. I am reminded of the provision in the constitutions of many of the southern states that voters must read, write and understand the constitution. One gentleman of dark complexion was asked if he knew what that meant, and he said, "Yes, sir, it means that this nigger isn't going to vote." These regulations mean that our people cannot take their products to a ready and customary market. The result is an unnecessary loss.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Referring shortly to my hon. friend's first question, as to whether or not the fact that the Canadian dollar is on parity with the United States dollar has not largely removed the necessity for this restriction, I would say that the answer is in the negative. We still need to conserve our United States dollar reserves, and that is the purpose of foreign exchange control. Prior to the change in the exchange rate, the Canadian exporter received more in Canadian dollars for the goods which he exported, but that is the only change which has taken place.
United States dollars seem to be in current circulation in Montreal these days.
Illegally.

This afternoon I listened to hon. gentlemen who were not satisfied with the legislation for returned men because it was not broad enough. I was reminded of denunciations of taxation which have been
made in previous times. When expenditures come before the house or before the committee they are all agreed upon; they are never enough. To-night I am thinking of the denunciation of bureaucracy. This bill is intended to increase bureaucracy. Hon. members have referred to a few cases where complaints could be lodged against the action of this board, but I am distressed by the fact that the hon. gentleman who sponsors this legislation has said that the export permits to be issued by the foreign exchange control board will not be the same as those issued by the Department of Trade and Commerce. This is another permit, something entirely different; it is not the same thing; it is something new. Then there will be other permits for imports different from those issued by the Department of Trade and Commerce.
There are four departments of government set up to promote trade between provinces or between Canada and other countries. The first of these is the Department of Agriculture. The next is the Department of Mines and Resources which supplies prospectors with maps, et cetera. Those two departments help the different producers in this country to develop trade. I remember the legislation passed by the Bennett government in connection with marketing between the provinces. That caused more trouble than could be described now, but the purpose was to develop trade through the Department of Agriculture.
Trade consists of exports and imports. To promote exports we have the Department of Trade and Commerce. This department has assisted Canadian producers and Canadian manufacturers; it has paid subsidies to navigation lines, et cetera. But on top of this department we have now set up a commercial corporation. This has been established by legislation, and unfortunately I was notjn the house on Monday when the particular legislation passed like butter in a pan. It was a new scheme thought up by a few of the intelligentsia to give direction to trade through the Department of Trade and Commerce. The long-established department was not enough; a corporation had to be set up on top.
We have had since confederation the former department of customs and excise, afterwards the Department of National Revenue, to deal with imports. There is another branch of that department, the bureau of statistics, which is supposed to do the work that is proposed to be done by this board. We have not heard from the bureau of statistics for a long time. I remember, when the Bennett government was in power, I used to receive

farm or the catch up to a value of $100 each month, but it would not relieve such exporters from the necessity of making the usual export entry.
In point of fact, this permit about which so much has been said, as to the nuisance of getting it, is issued by the customs officer and forms part of the forms in connection with customs export entries. It is known as form B, and the permit is obtained by filling out the usual customs export entry form, which now calls for a declaration by the exporter of the goods, their destination, the price to be received and so on.
The whole purpose of this permit system is to make sure that exports to foreign countries and in particular to the United States- that is what we are talking about now-will result in proceeds of sales being paid in United States dollars and made available to our exchange fund. That is the purpose of the permit. Under subsection 2 of section 25 it is provided-
The hoard shall not withhold a permit for the export of goods from Canada where payment of not less than the fair value of the goods in a currency designated by the board as acceptable for such a transaction,
(a)	has been received by a resident from a non-resident and, in the case of payment in foreign currency, the foreign currency has been sold to an authorized dealer;
or
(b)	is due to a resident from a non-resident under the terms of sale within six months after the goods are exported from Canada and. in case where payment is to be made in foreign currency, the board is satisfied that the foreign currency will be offered for sale to an authorized dealer forthwith upon receipt.
There is not any great hardship involved in that. There is not any great formality involved in it. It is true there may not be a customs officer close to the point where a particular farmer wishes to take his load of hay across the boundary line. Nevertheless, if he is selling hay or any other commodity in the United States he must make an export entry for that produce. He should be required to do so and he is required to do so. There is no additional formality in obtaining a permit of the foreign exchange control board, because customs officers act as agents of the board in issuing those permits.

The post offices were in the same building, the Canadian postmaster was for many years a faithful servant of the United States postmaster. To-night I am listening to this debate for the fifth time in less than a year. As I listen to it, I am reminded of the fact that we have already passed some eleven bills, ten of which I think deal specifically with the care of those who served in the armed forces. The whole ten of them have not generated as much heat either in committee or in this chamber as has this particular bill-and not just to-night.
I have been one of those who have, as recently as last week, and on various other occasions asserted myself for, and put forth claims on behalf of these fire fighters. But I am also one of those who have held and will continue to hold-and will make no apology for so doing-the view that there ought to be some measure of demarcation between that which is done for a civilian in any branch of the war effort and that done for those who were in the armed forces. In that I made one exception-I made it the other night, and I make it again now-and that is the case of the supervisors, which I shall not discuss now, but mention only to keep the record clear. I held the view then and I do now, that possibly there should be some differentiation between them and the fire fighters. But I am bound to say that I am not one who doubted or now doubts the fact that the fire fighters who left Ottawa to proceed overseas were in their own minds, and with justification, convinced that they had become without uniforms a part of the services.
Further to that, there was one observation made by an hon. member this afternoon-I

do not remember which one-where he said that the fire fighters had fought fires in England under the same disciplinary terms as those under which the armed forces were operating. So far as I know, that is the only wholly inaccurate statement made in the discussion this afternoon. I think it has some bearing-in my judgment it has-because I am-

As a member of the House of Commons, I am not completely happy-indeed I am not happy at all-about the situation which has arisen with respect to the fire fighters. I will be perfectly frank about it and say this, that, had it not been for the fact-to me it is a fact-that commitments were made-whether they were made with or without authority is beside the point at the present time, because they were not refuted by anybody who was in authority-I would not have urged in the committee, as I am prepared to urge here now that further consideration be given to those claims. But I am not prepared to go the whole way with this or any other group which is really a civilian organization. To my mind, there must be some point of discrimination between the volunteer military services and those who served, no matter how meritoriously, in any other branch of the war effort.
I do not intend to interject anything into this debate which will precipitate another discussion, but I am thinking of men who were test pilots and were never out of this country but who were engaged in an exceedingly dangerous occupation. I am thinking of those who worked on the ammunition dumps on our sea coasts and in the artillery camps. I was not much moved by the picture of a chap sitting on a ship loaded with bombs. People have been blown up in dumps and by explosions in our artillery camps. It seems to me too bad that this kind of emotionalism has crept into the debate. I would not suggest that the heat that has been engendered in debate is due to the name of the organization. I am inclined to think it grows out of the commitments made by certain members and perhaps by certain groups in the house before all the facts were fully before them.

The fact is that a veterans affairs committee was set up and, since all of us could not be on that committee, we put our trust in the capabilities of those who were appointed members of the committee. I think it is generally recognized that the members of the committee did a good job. On two different occasions the committee voted on the question whether these fire fighters were to be given the same benefits as the soldiers, and on both occasions the contention on behalf of these men was upheld and the committee passed it. But when it comes to the government they just disregard the committee's proposals entirely. They set aside its recommendation, notwithstanding that we as members of the house put our faith and reliance in the government to see that the returned fire fighters should get a fair deal.
It seems a queer state of affairs that we should set up a committee of the house to investigate thoroughly all these problems; and, when they take evidence from all parts of the country, when witnesses are brought in from every section, and when the committee in their considered judgment, arrived at on two occasions, declare that these benefits should be extended to these men, the government takes it upon its own responsibility to disregard these recommendations. I fear that the country will not take this too well. Further than that, I wish to join with those who protested on the grounds that General LaFleche made this promise. As the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) said a moment ago, no matter how the government may endeavour to use it as an excuse to get out, the fact remains that when General LaFleche was deputy minister he made the promise in order to get the fire fighters to enlist. Therefore they were bribed into enlisting under the pressure of something which they believed would be given. It cannot be considered in any other light than a deception on these men who put their faith in a government official of no less standing than a deputy minister. The Minister of Veterans Affairs excuses the government by saying, "Oh, well, we cannot be responsible for that." If that be true, then it was the duty of the government to dissociate themselves entirely from the remarks made by the deputy minister; otherwise the men who joined the corps were justified in taking the remark as being true, more particularly when they were going on a mission of life and death.
It would not have been difficult for the government to dissociate themselves from the
remark when they knew well that they had no intention of putting the promise into effect. It is not good enough for them to say now that it was given by an inferior member of the civil service. When the parliamentary assistant tries to imply that the fire fighters were not in as great danger as some of the others in the armed services he is belittling the work that these men did.

speechtext:
I am a member of the House of Commons. Perhaps that it enough. As I was saying, Mr. Speaker, I am 
surprised to see a measure of this sort brought in. I had always supposed that we granted rewards to our armed service personnel for certain considerations such as: that they had rendered service; that they had risked danger; that there had been disruption in their lives, with resultant financial and economic loss; that they had shown a willingness to place themselves at the complete disposal of the government, and so forth. In the case of these fire fighters, we find that these men have rendered excellent service. No one doubts that. They risked great dangers, loss of life and limb; their lives were disrupted, with resultant economic and financial loss. I know farmers who were in the fire-fighters corps who, in order to serve their country, disposed of their farms only to come back finding themselves with no farm. How were they to tell when they enlisted how long they would be called upon to serve? Finally, they had a willingness to go wherever they were told to go by the government of the country.
Under those circumstances, surely they have qualified for treatment similar to that which we accord to our fighting men. How can discrimination against them such as is contemplated in this bill be justified? It has been argued that General LaFleche. when he made the promise to these men, was only a civil servant. I see no disposition on the part of the government of Canada to treat lightly the pronouncements of Donald Gordon, who is also a servant of the government. His pronouncements seem to be surrounded by an air of sanctity.
It seems to me that the government has no defence for the position it has taken up in this bill, and, if this house is to reflect upon Canada that honour which it should reflect upon the country on this occasion, I believe it should ask the minister to withdraw the bill and reconstruct it in such a way as to give the men of this splendid corps treatment such as they have richly deserved.

I would be remiss in my duty if I did not add my protest to the passing of this bill now. Over a year ago, before the veterans affairs committee was set up, I had the pleasure of interviewing a number of fire fighters, and particularly the fire fighters of Calgary and that district, who came to me in regard to their case. I pointed out to them on that occasion that I felt certain a committee of the house would be set up to deal with the matter and, rather foolishly I think, judging by the way matters have turned out, I told them that I put a great deal of confidence in the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Mac-

War Service Benefits-Fire Fighters
Sir Aylmer . . . spoke glowingly of the work of the Canadian fire-fighter corps, "which fitted in awfully well, worked hard, did any job under the highest pressure and usually in the most dangerous spot.
Actually there were members of this corps killed and other members wounded in Great Britain. When the raids were on they had to be out on the streets. Evidence to that effect was given before the special committee on veterans affairs; and, as other members of the house have pointed out to-night, the veterans affairs committee recommended that these overseas fire fighters be accorded all benefits, pensions, rehabilitation rights and income tax exemption accorded to members of the armed forces. We had the question up the other day when considering income tax, and the Department of Finance have now agreed to treat these men in the same way as the auxiliary supervisors, those men sent over by the Canadian Legion, Y.M.C.A., Knights of Columbus and the Salvation Army; the firemen are now to get exemption for one-fifth of their income. Further, this very government last fall brought in a bill giving the men of the auxiliary services and the fire fighters exactly the same allowances. I have here the draft bill then submitted to the committee on veterans affairs, and it treats these two groups in exactly the same way. But this year it is different. The house this afternoon passed bill No. 325, which gives the supervisors of the auxiliary services all the rights of men in the forces with the exception of income tax exemption, but the bill for the fire fighters leaves out quite a few of these rights. In other words, the two groups are now being treated in a different way. I suggest to that house that that is not right, but that the fire fighters' bill should be in the same terms as the bill for the supervisors which was passed this afternoon ; and I would urge the minister, even at this late date, to comply with the recommendations made by the veterans affairs committee and treat these firemen just as though they had been members of the armed forces.

speechtext:
The parliamentary assistant has based his argument on the order in council which was passed in 1942, and which, he says, sets out the conditions that were to apply to these firemen. That order in council does not mean a thing, because it was passed after these men, or certainly after a great majority of them,

had been recruited, and neither the parliamentary assistant nor anyone else can properly contend that the men knew they were being recruited subject to those terms. He has made light of the promises given by Major General LaEleche, who at that time was deputy minister of national war services and was in charge of raising this corps of fire fighters. I have an affidavit here, sworn on August 3 in Windsor by Lester Barron, Robert Ferguson, Joseph Shilliday, Douglas Copeman, George T. Monk, Neil Brillinger, George Glabb and Donald Berneche, firemen, all of the city of Windsor in the county of Essex, and John Thornton, captain, fire department, Hedley G. 1.	That we were all members of the corps of Canadian fire fighters.

I am sure that everybody feels that this subject has been debated at considerable length. The fire fighters have
deserved a great deal of consideration and that is why we are extending their benefits under this act. It carries the benefits quite a step farther in regard to vocational and technical training and benefits under the Unemployment Insurance Act. That is to meet the recommendations of the committee. But it was felt by the government that there should be some distinction drawn between the man who placed himself or was placed by the law entirely at the disposal of the government

Wn)- Service Benefits-Fire Fighters
an O.B.E. for their work on behalf of the services because we have passed eight bills to-day. I want to pay a tribute to what the fire departments have done, not only overseas but here in Canada. According to a return I got in 1944, we had $4,500,000 worth of damage done by fire in our camps while the troops were in training during this war. That is a lot of money and much of that loss was not insured. There was a large fire at Camp Borden, and only for the fortunate fact that the wind was blowing in a certain direction many people might have been killed. The same thing happened in the maritimes.
Some tribute should be paid to the fire departments of the country. During the last two great wars these departments, along with the police and street departments, provided hundreds and hundreds of recruits, many of whom were wounded and many of whom did not return. These recommendations in connection with those who went overseas are most commendable. While I am dealing with this particular question, I might mention that we have a fine fire chief, George Sinclair, who has been on duty for a long time and he was passed over when the decorations were handed out. When we leave this mortal body and take on the immortal body I suppose a few letters after our name will not make much difference. I believe in paying tribute to the men who have worked in our fire departments both in peace and war. I remember that the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) when a student at Toronto university, used to cover the fire halls and police court when Colonel Dennison was the magistrate, as a reporter for the Globe and Mail, and he took a great interest in the department at the time of the disastrous fire of 1905 in Toronto in which the father of our able present mayor, R. H. Saunders, K.C., C.B.E., was badly injured.
In adopting this bill, parliament will be paying a tribute long overdue to a fine body of men who by day and by night risk their lives to protect the life and property of the citizens of our country.

I am another member of the committee who feels that I cannot let this bill go forward without recording that I also regret its present form. To be brief, may I put on the record that these fire fighters for overseas service were recruited under federal authority and were asked to serve in the United Kingdom, but so far as the men themselves were concerned they were prepared to go anywhere. Had they been asked to serve in Burma, India, the middle

east or anywhere else, it would have been the same thing to them. Sixty per cent of these men were trained fire fighters and they were directed into this corps because that was their trade. It may interest the house to know that a brigade of this fire-fighting corps embarked for France on D-day, but through some technicality they were recalled and did not enter France. But they never argued that that was not a part of their voluntary duties. I am sorry indeed that the government has not made good the promises which, if it did not put them in writing, were assumed to be a moral obligation on the part of the government, and I am sorry to see that these fire fighters are being penalized as to income tax, in benefits and even in decorations.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. A. TUCKER (Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs):

Mr. Speaker, there has been the suggestion that promises were made to the fire fighters when they went into the service. I have here a pamphlet issued by the king's printer in 1942, containing the regulations pertaining to the corps of (civilian) Canadian fire fighters for service in the United Kingdom, as approved by order in council, P.C. No. 76/1656 of 3rd March, 1942. It sets out exactly the terms under which these men were recruited and were supposed to serve. If anyone is interested, 1 have no doubt that he can get a copy from the king's printer.
The pamphlet also sets out what they were to receive on discharge. We hear a lot about what somebody is supposed to have told them, but this pamphlet sets out in writing what they were told they were to get upon discharge. It will be found at page 17 of this pamphlet, under the heading, "discharge":
Upon discharge, at the termination of his service or for medical unfitness or other cause, a member shall be provided with a transportation warrant to his home, together with such meal and lodging warrants as may be required. He shall be given a clothing allowance of thirty-five (35) dollars provided he has completed one hundred and eighty-three days of full service with the corps.
There is no suggestion whatsoever there that they were to be on the same basis as the armed services. But it does set down in writing the basis upon which this corps, which is definitely referred to as the (civilian) Canadian fire fighters for service in the United Kingdom, was raised.
In the face of what they were actually promised. I should like to put upon Hansard what is being done for the fire fighters. Incidentally I think we shall all admit that they did a good job. The head of the fire fighters in the United Kingdom wrote a letter

War Service Benefits-Fire Fighters
ing; we should be getting more than that." They will not be satisfied, and then we shall have trouble. But I shall not be responsible;
I shall tell them what occurred in this house, and Hansard will be there as a record to show that I foresaw what was necessarily going to happen.

subtopic: STATUTORY AUTHORITY FOR ORDERS IN COUNCIL PASSED UNDER WAR MEASURES ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased that the veterans affairs committee has seen fit to recommend to the government that increased benefits be provided for this handful of brave men, and I am pleased also that the government has seen fit to follow that recommendation. I have argued previously in this house the case of the fire fighters, taking the attitude that they should receive equal benefits with those men who are commonly called the combatant veterans. Like other hon. members, I attempted to prove, and I think I did with little difficulty, that in some cases their task was equally arduous and dangerous as that of the soldier in the front line. However, I shall not go into that now.
There is one question I should like to ask with reference to section 6. I think this shotdd be asked before we come to the section so that it may be passed at that time. I refer to vocational training. Prior to the war, some of these boys were not, as the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) has said, experienced firemen with technical training. Some of them were attending the universities of this country. I know one student of theology who enlisted. In the expectation that the benefits granted to the fire fighters would be increased, he went back to the university after returning from overseas and he has been there for a year. Perhaps I could have found out this information in another way, but I should like a definition of vocational and. technical training benefits referred to in section 6. I should like that defined in terms of university work such as I have described. As I understand it, it would not cover university work; that, as it now stands, it means training a man to work with his hands for the purpose of fitting him to make his own living.	-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: STATUTORY AUTHORITY FOR ORDERS IN COUNCIL PASSED UNDER WAR MEASURES ACT
speechtext: It does not cover it.

subtopic: STATUTORY AUTHORITY FOR ORDERS IN COUNCIL PASSED UNDER WAR MEASURES ACT
speechtext:
All I can say is that I am very much disappointed. I do not see why a young lad at the university should not receive the same benefits. Unfortunately many people think of education as being vocational training only, and I had something to say about that in the budget debate. This man who is taking up theology or a man who is taking up an arts course to become a
teacher, should be encouraged, and I appeal that these benefits be extended to cover the cases I have cited.

subtopic: STATUTORY AUTHORITY FOR ORDERS IN COUNCIL PASSED UNDER WAR MEASURES ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I regret that the government has seen fit to bring in this bill in its present form, because I am satisfied the majority of the fire fighters will look upon it as being a breach of faith. Furthermore, it is in direct opposition to the wishes of the veterans committee. The veterans committee gave this question a lot of consideration. They listened to briefs by the fire fighters on two occasions and, as a result, came to certain definite conclusions. One of them was that the full benefits of veterans legislation should be made available to the fire fighters. It is well to remember that on two occasions a vote was taken and that each time the vote was in favour of full benefits being given to the fire fighters. This bill is being brought into the house in direct conflict to the wishes of the veterans committee. ^
I think the reason the veterans committee took this stand was obvious. In the first place they felt that the government was under direct obligation to make these benefits available in view of the fact that General ijaFleche, then deputy minister of war services, had made that promise to the men upon their enlisting. The second reason is that, when they enlisted, the battle of Britain was on, and it was believed that these men would face hazards just as great as those faced by the men in the armed forces. If it is argued that the hazards to be faced by these men decreased greatly and their job became easier as a consequence and, therefore, they should not receive the full benefits, then I would point out that the same might be argued regarding many of the men who served in the armed forces.
An important point to remember is that these men volunteered for service overseas on the plea of the government. In many respects we treat the man who never went outside Canada more generously than we are treating the fire fighters. These fire fighters enlisted and went overseas, and it was not their fault that the blitz subsided and the work they had to do was less hazardous than was expected. Why should they be penalized_ because of that fortunate situation? I submit that, when a pledge was given by the government to men going overseas, that pledge should be kept and not broken merely for the sake of saving a few dollars.

subtopic: STATUTORY AUTHORITY FOR ORDERS IN COUNCIL PASSED UNDER WAR MEASURES ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the bill which is before us now is one of the most important we have had this session. I think the least that could be done is to grant all the members of this committee

War Service Benefits-Fire Fighters
retraining overseas to fit them to do the fine job they did could not have cost very much. When they went over they were fit and qualified to do their job. As a citizen of Toronto, I cannot, of course, be criticized for taking pride in the Toronto fire department, the job it has done in peace time, the masterly job it has done through the years, and what this large number of volunteers did overseas.
I know a number of these men-I have the names of nine of them here-and I shall close what I have to say by putting on record the names of these outstanding and practical firemen of Toronto. They are Dick Hake, Tom Kendall, Jim Gow, Tom Hogg, Charles Rown-tree, Jr., A. Blackburn, M.M.-it will be noted that this man had won the military medal- Dick Wood, Dave Maxwell and Herb Magill.
Mr. JEAN-FRANCOIS POULIOT (Temis-couata): Mr. Speaker, I wish to congratulate the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Mac-Nicol) upon the fine speech he has made. As a Canadian I am proud of the fire brigade in Toronto, just as I am of the fire brigade in every other city across Canada. However, under the able leadership of my honourable and very dear friend the member for Broadview (Mr. Church) the fire brigade of Toronto was particularly well organized.
My hon. friend's remarks bring to mind those cities which have chosen the most able men in every field of activity, so that the business of those cities might prosper and the taxpayers pay the least possible in taxes. One realizes when he goes to Toronto that the two most popular men there are, precisely, the hon. member for Broadview and the hon. member for Davenport. Even the taxi drivers speak highly of them, and I am sure many of them know no other men in public life than my_ two hon. friends. Surely that is some reward for their years of service and their accomplishments on behalf of the common people.
We have seen the Canadian fire fighters at work in front of this building, and we know they did exceptionally well. However, there is one thing that strikes me, and that is that the fire brigades have been so well organized in the various cities of Canada that it was possible for them to take the risk of sending some of their members overseas to fight the fires in the large cities of the British isles, and particularly in London. Those men deserve great credit. As a young boy I was always interested in where the fire brigade was going; we were always like that, and I believe we still are. Many people go to the window to look at them when they pass. Those men are well 
trained and do their work well. This is not only a tribute to the heads of municipal councils who have provided1 all our cities and towns with excellent fire protection, but also a tribute to the people of Canada who have taken upon themselves the risk of sending overseas for the protection of the British isles against fires precisely those men who were needed at home. Not only the municipal authorities but also the people of Canada generally should be commended upon that act of generosity. I wonder if the same thing would have been done by other countries if Canada had1 been exposed to bombardment similar to that which cursed the British isles. However, we must give everyone the benefit of the doubt.
Since those men did so well, I cannot see why the British government does not fix them up so that they will get from the United Kingdom, which has been showered with so many gifts of money from Canada, some reward. I admire the firemen. They went over there and assumed great risks, They did so for civilization, and for the civilization of the British isles. I wonder why the British government comes again to Canada begging-no, they did not come to Canada this time; they are reluctant to come-but the firemen are being helped by this country just because they were not given enough by the United Kingdom government. Here again I protest against this kind of legislation. I do not do this because I am not in favour of the firemen. I admire them just as much as do the hon. members for Broadview and Davenport and all my colleagues in this house. I admire them and realize that they deserve a lot, but that lot should come to them from England and not from Canada. That is my point of view.
This reminds me of the father-and I use a metaphor to illustrate my point-who had numerous children who were crying for bananas. He got sick and tired of hearing them, so that he decided to buy a large bunch of bananas. The children started to eat bananas that day and they had plenty of them and finally ate the whole bunch. Then the father bought another bunch and, after they had eaten a few of that bunch, they were all sick of them; they had eaten too much. The same thing is likely to happen to the men for whom this legislation is designed. They may get too much; they may become fed up with it all, and it will cause trouble.
After Jean Francois Pouliot has protested, it will be the men themselves who will show their dissatisfaction. I had an example not long ago of a boy who said to me, "We are getting only $60 a month for vocational train-

service considered then to be as dangerous as that performed by any human being in the British isles, whether in uniform or not.
At the next session of parliament he had this to say on April 24, 1944, as reported at page 2323 of Hansard:

In conclusion, may I say that I want it clearly understood that I am not one who is merely advocating a greater government expenditure. I have never done that and I hope I shall never be guilty of it. I put forth these arguments merely because, in my opinion, these promises were made by a responsible representative of the government. subtopic: STATUTORY AUTHORITY FOR ORDERS IN COUNCIL PASSED UNDER WAR MEASURES ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Wentworth (Mr. Lennard) did such a good job that he left very little for anyone to say. I compliment him upon his contribution on behalf of all the firemen who participated in the serious work for which they volunteered overseas. But I would be derelict in my duty if I were not to say something about those gallant and efficient men who volunteered from the Toronto fire department to go overseas. I might say, Your Honour, there was a considerable number of them, and of that number a large proportion enlisted from Davenport riding.
I have used the word "efficient", because the captain of the Toronto fire department, Captain George Sinclair, is known throughout America as a chief who is efficient and who has raised high the position of Toronto firemen on this continent. Before proceeding to say what I intend to say, I should add that, during his seven years as mayor of Toronto, the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) was to a great extent responsible for the high standard of efficiency of the fire brigade in that city.
To-day I received a letter from one of the fire fighters in Toronto who enlisted and went
overseas. It is not my intention to read the letter, but only to state briefly what is contained in it. They are not complaining. They volunteered; they went over there to do their duty and were proud to have that opportunity. Some of them were wounded, while others made the supreme sacrifice. But, with all that, they were all gallant men who were proud to render a service during a great war.
This man tells me in his letter, however, that he and his buddies were away for two years, eight months and eleven days, or a total of 999 days. This particular correspondent's pay from the Toronto fire department, which pays good wages to its men was $2,624 a year. In the 999 days he was away, had he been home at his job with the Toronto fire department he would have earned $7,021, or within a dollar or so of (that amount. While in the service he received $2.70 a day, with $35 a month separation allowance for his wife, or $3,942 for the 999 days he was absent. This meant a depletion in his income, or what would have been his income if he had remained at home, of $3,079. He tells me that he received-I presume as a gratuity, although I. am not quite sure what it is called-(the sum of $465. This means a net loss to that Toronto fireman-and, for all I know, to all of those Toronto men who enlisted-of $2,614.
The bill does say that, if they wish to have it, these men will receive vocational training and unemployment insurance. But to the professional firemen on the Toronto fire brigade those two items are of little significance. They will not require unemployment insurance because their positions are permanent. Then, the men in that fire department received sick leave, and all those other things which go along for the benefit of those who work for a city which pays its men as the Toronto city council pays the men of that city. Nor will they require vocational training.
I have been wondering what the department will give those men in place of vocational training and unemployment insurance. They suggest that they be granted the benefits of the Veterans Land Act which, as I understand it, would entitle them to assistance, provided that they took over a small lot close to the city. Some of them, of course, are pensioners. There is a suggestion that they be given reestablishment grants. I am not conversant enough with what the minister has in mind to pass comment upon it, but I am just passing on this information as it has been given to me.
Those men who went from the Toronto fire department-and I have no doubt the same would apply to others who went from other fire departments-were well trained. Their

War Service Benefits-Fire Fighters
what they knew best and they gave to that service their best. Several of these fire fighters were married men. with families and would never have been called up by the armed services in any event.
I am sure that what I have said applies to all fire fighters who went overseas, some 400. They volunteered at a time when the national defence tax was being deducted at the source. None, however, was deducted from them. The same thing applied when income tax deductions were made at the source. If they were to have been taxed, the government as their employer erred badly in not deducting that tax. Those who paid the national defence tax for the early part of 1942 received rebates from the government. I wish to point out to the house that none of these deductions made by the Department of National Revenue were made at the source.
These men were all on the same footing as the Canadian army overseas. They came home and were discharged, and months after that they received notices from the revenue department-the good old revenue department-that they owed so-and-so in back income taxes. That is a fine reception, a grand finale to a job well done.
It is repeatedly stated that the corps was limited to service in the United Kingdom. I wish to quote a portion of paragraph 3, part I of the regulations, which reads as follows: Purpose of corps-
3.	The corps shall assist the national fire service in Great Britain in-
By the way, Mr. Speaker, the corps was considered by the British government as a fourth arm of the service and was on the same footing as those in the armed services. I continue:
The corps shall assist the national fire service in Great Britain in (1) the extinction of fires, and the protection of life and property in case of fire, in Great Britain, Northern Ireland and the Isle of Man; (2) the extinction of fires and the protection of life and property in ships and vessels at sea.
There is no restriction there. There was no limitation to their duties at sea, apparently.
Another angle that I wish to emphasize is that these overseas fire fighters were asked to volunteer to proceed to France on or after V-E day. The entire overseas force volunteered for this special duty, and from them were picked 100 men who were specially trained and attached to the 21st army group, and were ready to leave for France on V-E day. They were on the boat or on landing barges and they were taken off. They were fully trained and had army personnel attached to them in a liaison capacity. The only thing that pre-

vented them from seeing duty on the continent was the mere fact that the raids in France did not develop as was expected.
Another matter that I feel should be emphasized i3 the fact that of the overseas personnel three were killed, five seriously wounded, three wounded, and twenty-seven are at the present time receiving pension. Some hoped to receive treatment. This is being denied them under the bill.
As is often the case, a man who served overseas with the corps applies to the civil service commission for a position as fireman. I know of one or two cases where this has happened. What happens when he applies for that position? He is turned down. Why? Because he is told that he was not a member of the armed service. He is told that, despite the fact that he is a full-fledged and experienced fireman who has served overseas. He is told that, because he was not with the armed service, he can get no civil service preference.
These fire fighters have received recognition from the British government in the award of the defence of Britain decoration. They have quite recently, as announced by the Minister of Veterans Affairs, been promised the latest service decoration, the war medal. I would urge that the government give consideration to awarding them the general service medal. This medal has been worn by all those in the service whether they left Canada or not, and I feel that these fire fighters who went over and did their bit should be extended that privilege. I hold in my hand an editorial which appeared in the Toronto Daily Star of August 1. This is a paper which usually supports the government, and has done so in recent years. I shall not read the whole article because we want to get along.

I may observe in passing that, with the exception of one or two important debates, if speakers were limited to twenty minutes the affairs of the house would be conducted in a more businesslike manner. I fully realize that this is the bill, and it will go through as it stands, regardless of what I have to say, but I cannot allow this opportunity to pass without pointing out certain facts.
In volunteering to do the job they were best equipped for, men from the Canadian fire departments answered the call of the dominion government, and accepted the dominion government's terms without question, just as volunteers did in any other service. They offered their lives if necessary, their limbs and their health. Their term of duty was for the war's duration, or as long as required, just the same as the armed troops. It has been said by a present responsible minister of the crown that the reason fire fighters did not receive full recognition was that they could resign from the service at any time they wished. I have a copy of a letter written in reply to a communication from a controller in Toronto which would lead one to believe that the members of the cabinet council, or some of them, did not have the actual facts before them, because regulation 30 reads:
A member may be required to serve for the duration of the present war or as long thereafter as his services may be needed.
These men accepted comparable ranks and pay, the same allowances for their wives and families; they received the same treatment as regards medical examinations, medical care, pensions, discipline, clothing, feeding, travel, right down to the smaller items such as carrying Canadian army cards, being photographed and finger-printed by the Canadian army, and receiving similar discharge csrtification on discharge. Before these men went overseas, they were promised by Major General LaFleche, then deputy minister of war services-and he made the statement on more than one occasion, because these men left in drafts of fifty or so-that they would receive all the advantages that would be granted to the armed forces.
It has been said that some of these overseas fire fighters were conscientious objectors and had joined the fire-fighting corps to evade the army call-up. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have no objection to the amendments, so far as they go, to the War Service Grants Act which are covered by this bill. There has been criticism that some of the amendments do not go far enough. Some are merely clarifications and nothing need be said about them.
There are four amendments which amount to anything. Two of them deal with gratuities, particularly the supplementary gratuity, and the other two deal with reestablishment credits. The ones dealing with gratuities mainly provide that a man who joins the permanent or interim force and takes a reduction in rank to do so shall not thereby lose part of the gratuity to which he would otherwise be entitled. That, I think, is sound and fair, and we are entirely in agreement with it. The other amendment dealing with gratuities fixes a cut-off date for men who join the permanent or interim force. There is no criticism of that. The third amendment deals with the extension to the widow of a soldier who may have died of the right to his reestablishment credit if the veteran had not drawn it before his death. That is a provision with which we are wholly in accord, and in my opinion it should have been written into the act to begin with. At the same time it impresses me as unfair that, because a man did the country a service by not drawing his reestablishment credit immediately, his wife should be penalized if he happened to die before he had occasion to use that credit. The only criticism I have is that I think the privilege should have been extended to the man's children. The amendment only provides that it may go to the widow and the dependent mother. The case of a man with dependent children, whose wife or whose mother is dead might well have been covered in the amendment, and I hope that that will be done at some future time. The fourth amendment is with regard to the use of the reestablishment credit to enable a veteran to pay off indebtedness on his home. Previously he had only been able to use this credit up to twice the amount which he himself paid. That is now being improved in that he can use it up to twice the amount paid, even though it was paid some years in the past. That also, I think, should have been liberalized so that it would not have been necessary to limit the amount of this reestablishment credit that he could use to twice the amount he paid himself. That is another change in the act which I would also hope to see instituted.

Therefore the lack of fulfilment of the minister's statement merely had the effect of disappointing the veterans without meeting the situation.
In the light of these facts, it is interesting to look at the statistics as to the number of veterans who have left universities since the inception of the plan. These statistics will be found at page 1407 of the proceedings of the veterans affairs committee, and they show that 2,470 students have discontinued their courses, of which number nine left for financial reasons, while 841 left to take jobs before completing their courses. In view of the information given the committee by the organizations which presented briefs, it is a safe assumption that these students left, not because they preferred to take jobs rather than to complete their course, but because they had to take the jobs for the reason that they were financially unable to complete the courses. This means that 850 out of 2,470 left for straight financial reasons or because they had to take jobs. In other words, thirty-one per cent of the total number up to 63260-283
that date left for financial reasons. The information we have is that a great many more will leave this summer. I have heard that the number will be as high as fifty per cent in some universities. However, that is in the future. I have given the statement that was made by the students themselves, and we have no figures on which to base definite predictions for the future.
Unfortunately, the only amendment we can move to take care of the situation is one that would involve the expenditure of public funds. It was urged that the grant for married veterans be increased to $100. The attempt we are making to-day is to show that the act, as it stands at present or as it is about to be amended, will not take care of the position of the married men at the universities who are running behind at the rate of $40 a month.
I would conclude by urging the minister to fulfill the implication contained in his speech as reported in the newspapers on June 27, so that veterans may be able to take advantage of the legislation and we shall not be in the position of spending a great deal of money on veterans and having it wasted because the veteran is unable to complete his course, because those who have looked into the situation are convinced that large numbers will be forced to discontinue their courses. In conclusion, student veterans, and especially married, have adopted every means possible to keep going. speechtext:
The whole underlying policy of government legislation for veterans

Veterans Business Loans
section 1 of the War Service Grants Act contains almost the same definition of business as there is in this bill. That was done because we felt that these are companion pieces of legislation and should be more or less the same in their provisions as to where the money could be invested. That is one reason why it was felt that they should be permitted to use their reestablishment credit- to buy into a partnership or to buy an interest in a business, but not to buy shares in a corporation. It was felt the restrictions should be the same.
Our department, which has had a great deal of experience in the reestablishment of veterans, felt strongly that veterans should not be exposed to the possibility of somebody coming to them and getting them to go to a bank to borrow money with which to buy an interest in a corporation. We felt that we might be exposing veterans to pressure from unscrupulous persons. They might have a tendency to throw their reestablishment credit into some business and lose everything.
It was not pressure from the financial institutions that decided the government; it was advice from Major General Burns, our director of rehabilitation, and the deputy minister, that decided the government. The government felt they would be wrong in not taking that advice, that they should not permit this act to be used to buy shares in corporations. In following that advice we felt that we were following the best advice we could get.
There has been some question as to why there should be a guarantee of only ten per cent in the case of farmers who are going to farm under the Farm Improvement Loan Act when there is a guarantee of twenty-five per cent of the first million of loans made by banks under this bill. The answer is that the whole basis of this act is to help the veteran who has enlisted and who may have been overseas for five years when he would not have an opportunity to- build up a relationship with his bank manager. When this man comes back he is almost a stranger, and it was felt that the government should give a form of partial guarantee of his loan. This is an altogether different proposition from a farmer getting a loan, because the farmer is generally well known. This higher guarantee is given not to help the banks, because w'e know they will do business in such a way as not to throw away their money; it was done so that credit, should be freely available to worthy veterans. If a bank can lend a million dollars and if one-quarter of those loans are guaranteed, it obviously means that the
veteran with any reasonable proposition can hope to get a loan. This is a most advantageous piece of legislation for any veteran going into business.
Some question has been raised about cutting down the rate of interest. I am just as anxious as any one to see rates of interest kept low, but I think it would be a poor way of serving the best interests of the veteran if you said to him that he could get a loan, say of $3,000, under this act and be charged three per cent instead of five per cent, which would so.ve him $60, and then have the bank decide that they could not work under that arrangement no matter what the guarantee might be. The bank might consider that they would lose money on it and refuse to make any loans at all. That would be an amazing way to help the veteran.

the Veterans Land Act, legislation which in part would give them a grant, and then a loan at a reasonable rate of interest of not more than three and one-half per cent.
While no doubt this legislation will help, nevertheless, as I have said, it will be a great disappointment to the veterans of Canada. Under it no grant is made, although I understand a veteran will be eligible for a reestablishment credit. It is stated however that the rate of interest will be five per cent. I cannot understand why we can help set a veteran up on a farm at three and one-half per cent, in addition give him a grant of $2,300, and then say to the veteran who wishes to begin a business, "We will not give you a grant, but we will soak you five per cent interest." As the hon. member for Weyburn has pointed out, these veterans are not to get. even the ^benefits a civilian gets when he asks for a farm improvement loan. He can borrow money *nt five per cent, with the government putting up only ten per cent, whereas in this instance they guarantee the chartered banks up to twenty-five per cent of their aggregate losses.
During the war we heard a great deal about the patriotic services rendered by the chartered banks in helping to do this and that. The war is over, and I think the banks might very well prove their sense of patriotism by letting the veterans have these loans at a rate of three per cent, thereby giving them a little more help. If the banks are not prepared to do that, I suggest it is a service the government might very well perform.
A short time ago we made provision in this house for loans to foreign countries at the rate of two per cent. The reason given for that low rate of interest was that these countries could not afford to pay more. Many applications for loans by veterans are being turned down on the groundi that they will not be able to meet their obligations. If it is found that a veteran is not able to meet his obligations under this act, should not the rate of interest be reduced on the same ground that we are making money available to foreign countries at the rate of two per cent? There is no suggestion of that kind at all. Why are we so liberal in making loans to foreign countries at two per cent when we refuse to treat our own veterans in a decent manner?
The hon. member for Weyburn suggested that the government might well consider reducing the rate of interest on these loans to three and a half per cent as a maximum, and then if the banks will not accept that responsibility the government should make the loans themselves. After all, during the war the gov-

This was very carefully considered by our committee, and it is quite true that the. committee finally recommended that this change be made. The government has had the advice of the director general of rehabilitation, who carefully considered the matter, and of the deputy minister, and their feeling is very strong that we should not agree to this change. As has been pointed out, the veteran must pay one-third of the total amount of the investment. Most veterans will have to use their reestablishment credit in order to do this. The reestablishment credit provisions were before the house, and our committee, and it was decided that we should not permit the veteran to use his reestablishment credit to purchase shares in an incorporated company. It was felt that a veteran might be lured into buying shares in an incorporated company, perhaps on the promise of getting a job, and then, having no control over the company after he had invested his reestablishment credit he might find that for some reason or another he was dismissed and would lose any benefit from the reestablishment credit. So we did not recommend that they have the right to use the reestablishment credit to purchase shares.
There was also the danger that they might be exposed to all kinds of pressure to buy shares in various companies. Section 2, sub-

Veterans Business Loans
suggestion by the hon. member for Vancouver South to allow veterans to purchase interests in incorporated companies, or to allow them to establish such companies. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am sure the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) did not wish to imply that only supporters of the government and the official opposition had anything to do with the preparation of this legislation.

speechtext: No.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY GRANTS TO UNIVERSITIES
speechtext:
As a matter of fact both C.C.F. and Social Credit groups played their full part on the veterans affairs committee, and I believe our record for attendance was good. Moreover, while I am definitely in favour of the principle in the bill, I am not in favour of the banks being granted the privilege-and I use that word advisedly-of being able to charge a five per cent interest rate. The banks have argued that of necessity the loans will be small, and that they will be spread from coast to coast. They point out that in most instances repayment will be on a monthly basis, and that therefore the costs of administration will be high. Let me point out that the great majority of loans made by banks are small; any bank manager will say that. They are widespread, too. Every bank manager handles such loans, and veterans' loans will not require any more attention than average small business loans will.
A local bank manager always investigates a loan before he will make it, and most loans are repayable on a monthly basis. For these reasons I cannot understand why a rate of five per cent should be charged, and six per cent on loans in default. In fact, six per cent is the legal maximum; they could not charge more if they wanted to. Anyone knows that he can go into a bank almost anywhere and obtain a loan at five per cent. At the present time veterans can obtain loans at three and one-half per cent from the Department of Veterans Affairs for the purchase of land. Why is the government not handling business loans in the same manner, either through the Department of Veterans Affairs or through the industrial development bank?

General measures which might be taken during an epidemic are: First, general warning to physicians and people generally of the prevalence of the disease, and warning of parents to report all suspicious cases for immediate medical care. Second, all children with fever should be isolated in bed pending diagnosis. Third, protection of children as far as practicable against unnecessary contact with other persons and crowds, avoiding all unnecessary visiting and travelling. Fourth, maintenance of general health of all children at as high a level as possible, with rest periods.
For the general information of the house I may say that not a great deal of progress has been made in the treatment of infantile paralysis. The new drugs which people speak of so much nowadays, sulpha drugs and penicillin, are absolutely powerless against the ravages of poliomyelitis. The disease is caused by what is known as a virus, and these dings do not appear to have any effect upon that particular virus. It would appear that the disease itself occurs in cycles, because the virus increases in virulence over a period of four or five years. Other methods of>
treatment which have been discarded have been the injection of human serum taken from the spinal cord of patients who have made a recovery. That is not giving the beneficial results which had been hoped for. I hope that people will not place too much reliance in the new drug called curare, which in isolated cases has given results but which has not been generally tested sufficiently to warrant the assertion that it has specific curative powers. For that reason it is to be hoped that people will not put too much confidence in it.
I am apprehensive that this may be one of the cycle years and in view of the fact that the epidemic has reached enormous proportions at this time in the United States, there is grave danger of there being a considerable increase in the number of cases in Canada.
I do not know that any better advice can be given than to tell people generally to follow the precautions that we have outlined, and that children, who are the principal victims, should be kept away from crowds and given plenty of rest and that their lives should be so regulated as not to give them too much exercise.
