Mr. Speaker, may I have the permission of the house to make a brief statement with reference to a question which was asked yesterday by the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon)? Yesterday the hon. member for Peel asked a question with reference to the increase of cases of infantile paralysis in certain sections of Canada, and wished a statement on the present
situation and what steps can be taken in connection with the spread of the epidemic. He also asked for a report on the number of cases and the comparison with the number in previous years when the epidemic was at its height in Canada.
I can well understand the concern of the hon. gentleman, as well as that of the Canadian people generally who recall the devastating effects of previous epidemics. This matter is of increasing importance to Canadians in view of the fact that the epidemic is sweeping sections of the United States, and our proximity to that country gives us reason for fear that the epidemic may spread to Canada.
Infantile paralysis is a peculiar disease, in that it appears to run in cycles of years. The greatest incidence of the disease in recent years was in 1941, when there were between January 1 and July 31 of that year two hundred and two cases. In 1937, it was regarded as epidemic in Ontario from the middle of August until the middle of October. In 1941 it was regarded as epidemic in Manitoba and New Brunswick from the middle of July to the middle of September.
I will now give you the total number of cases occurring in Canada from January 1 to July 31 for the years 1937 to 1946:	1937,
130; 1938, 139; 1939, 85; 1940, 47; 1941. 202; 1942, 111; 1943, 43; 1944, 88; 1945, 67; and to the end of July, 1946, 155 cases have been reported.
The control and treatment of poliomyelitis falls within the jurisdiction of the provinces and the municipalities. The dominion Department of Health and Welfare can act only by extending any assistance in its powder upon request of the province. Actual control and treatment of the disease is primarily a matter for municipal authorities acting along general lines of the regulations of the municipality and of the province.
Methods of control may be classified under two headings. First, as respects the infected individual. We suggest encouragement of as early recognition of the disease as possible. When the disease is epidemic, measures are taken to make consultant and laboratory services easily available to medical practitioners. Those laboratories are both provincial and dominion laboratories. Second, the hospitalization of the sick as far as this is possible, with isolation of the patient for from two to three weeks. Third, disinfection of discharges from the nose, throat and bowels, and of soiled articles. Fourth, investigation as far as possible of the sources of infection to locate unrecognized and unreported cases of the disease.

I shall not give his name, because I should like to place on record the actual decision rendered in the matter. I do not think his name was given by the hon. member.
This gentleman was serving on a ship which was certified by the Department of Transport

to be a ship of Canadian registry. On June 2, 1943, he met with an accident on board ship which resulted in amputation of his leg. Following upon the accident he was admitted to hospital and apparently was discharged on January 27, 1944.
An official of the immigration branch at Halifax telephoned the commission's representative, the pension medical examiner, and asked if he was interested in the case. Doctor Henderson, the examiner, thought it would be wise to carry out an examination and so obviate the possibility of any delay. This examination took place on January 26. The seaman was supplied with the necessary application form and the provisions for merchant seamen with regard to pension were fully explained to him.
The completed application form was received by the commission on February 24, 1944. Five days later the commission wrote to the Department of Transport requesting official advice regarding the registry of the vessel, whether the applicant was a member of the crew, and particulars regarding the operating company. On the same day the commission wrote to the seaman acknowledging the application, advising that it was receiving attention and requesting advice from him as to whether his statement that the accident occurred during a blackout referred to a general blackout in the area or during one on board the ship. He was advised at that time that his eligibility would hinge on the question whether the disability resulted from extraordinary marine peril consequent upon the existence of a state of hostilities. On the same day the commission made further inquiries with regard to the treatment which had been carried out at the marine hospital at Halifax and as to the extent of his disability.
When the necessary details were before the commission they were very carefully reviewed, and on May 12, 1944, the following decision was rendered:
According to the information available to the commission this applicant fell and injured his right leg on June 2, 1943, and later the leg had to be amputated. He alleges that the injury was sustained when he fell down a stoke-hole during a blackout aboard the ship. This contention is not borne out by the extract from the official log book which states that he was the worse for liquor all during the evening of June 2 and had fallen over a settee on the deck, and about 11.30 p.m. was found on the floor of the stoke-hole-leg broken.
In the opinion of the commission it has not been established that the injury was due to enemy action as defined by the terms of order in council P.C. 104-3546 and. the application, therefore, is not granted.
In view of this decision the commission has not taken action to confirm the applicant's statement that the ship was convoying iron ore

Personally I think a special bill should be prepared covering Canadian merchant seamen, extending to [DOT]them the benefits of rehabilitation as in the case of the armed services and the auxiliary services. In my opinion no one who went through the war is more entitled to consideration than the merchant seamen, because they certainly took it on the chin. They had no glory, they had no uniforms, they got no medals, they spent a lot of time on rafts in the ocean and all that kind of thing, and at this stage of the game the least we can do for them is to give them the rights of rehabilitation as we have done for the armed and auxiliary services.
As to pensions, I have something specific to say. It is difficult for a Canadian merchant seaman to secure a pension. I have a case in point, and the best illustration is the way in which the act is being administered. I have here two letters which I think pretty well cover the point. They show the runaround that the merchant seaman gets in all these matters because he is not looked upon as one who had anything to do with the war. Here is a statement from a boy who has a disability. He suffered the loss of a leg. The letter reads:
Sydney Mines, N.S., 5 April, 1946.
Mr. G. L. C. Johnson,
Director of Merchant Seamen,
95 Rideau Street,
Ottawa, Ontario.
Dear Sir:
On June 3, 1943, while serving as a merchant seaman aboard the steamship Phillip T. Dodge in Sydney, Cape Breton, Nova Scotia, I suffered an accident which later necessitated the amputation of my right leg. Particulars of the case are as listed hereunder:
On June 3, 1943, while the ship was in Sydney harbour, unloading, I accidentally fell into the stoke hole. I was admitted to Sydney City Hospital on June 3, 1943. Amputation was effected 4 October. 1943 and I was transferred to the Halifax Infirmary on November 8, 1943, where I remained under treatment for approximately four months. Later, on return to Sydney Mines it was necessary to be admitted to the
Sydney Merchant Marine Hospital and again to the Halifax Infirmary for checkup and further treatment.
The steamship Phillip T. Dodge is owned by the Waterman Steamship Company, registered in Saint John, New Brunswick, and at the time of my accident was chartered by the Dominion Steel and Coal Company.
Prior to this accident I was actively engaged as a merchant seaman, in dangerous waters aboard Canadian ships for several years.
He concludes by asking whether the director of merchant seamen would advise him of the procedure he should follow in order to qualify for a pension. The answer he received was written on June 28, 1946-and it will be remembered that this boy suffered his accident in 1943. This is what they say:
Ottawa, June 28, 1946.
Dear Sir:
I regret very much that there has been such a delay in replying to your letters but I have been daily expecting a reply to the inquiries I made regarding your case, to the Canadian pension board.
They have confirmed to me that your appeal for pension was duly considered but on full investigation of the circumstances surrounding your accident on board the Phillip T. Dodge it was found that it was not within their power to grant you a pension. Inasmuch as you are not pensionable it is also impossible for you to be considered for a vocational training grant.
It is indeed unfortunate that such an accident occurred to you but from the facts now ascertained it would appear that your accident resulted not through the line of duty but it was through your own personal liability that you suffered the loss of your limb.
I assure you that I greatly sympathize with you in your predicament but there seems to be absolutely no way in which assistance may be given to you.
I have written to the minister with reference to the case and I do not suppose he has had a chance to check it up. That was only on August 7. I have asked him to check with the commission and ascertain on what basis they made the decision.

Mr. G. . R. PEARKES (Nanaimo): Mr. Speaker, this bill covers a very wide group of persons who actively engaged in war work in various civilian capacities, ranging from merchant seamen and salt-water fishermen, personnel of the various auxiliary services which were helping the troops, members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, air raid precaution workers, members of civilian air crews and a large number of other groups.
Members of this house who were privileged to sit on the committee on veterans affairs listened to the briefs which were presented by the representatives of these various organizations. In every case their representatives told a story of high endeavour prompted solely by the loftiest of principles. The greatest reward which the individuals in these various groups expected to receive was the knowledge of a voluntary duty accepted and that duty efficiently and adequately performed. In their

Allied Veterans Benefits
It was of great value to the allied cause to have these different national units available when the liberation of Europe came about. Troops were identified as Polish, as Belgian, as French, as Norwegian, and as Dutch. It was a great thing for the nationals of those countries to feel that their own forces had been kept in being and that they had fought for freedom on the outside and were now coming to liberate their own countries. I understand that in a great many of these cases the government has endeavoured to arrange set-offs or reciprocal benefits with the countries with which we were allied. I hope the Canadian government and the Minister of Veterans Affairs will continue to arrange these reciprocal benefits.
It has been stated clearly that it is the government's intention that no man shall be included under these benefits who was not domiciled in Canada before going into the forces of an allied country, and that no man shall have these benefits if he does not indicate his intention to take up his domicile in Canada upon discharge from the forces. In other words, it takes into consideration only those members of the allied forces who were m Canada on September 10, 1939 and who have returned to Canada to make their homes here.
Mr. JEAN-FRANQOIS POULIOT (Temis-couata): Mr. Speaker, this bill is another instance of the policy put into force by the Meighen government after the war to give preference to men who were not in the Canadian army and who were taking the place of good Canadians who were in the Canadian army. The definition of "allied veteran" is as follows:
"Allied veteran" means a person who, subsequent to the tenth day of September, 1939, served in the armed forces of any of the nations allied with His Majesty in active operations against the enemy in the war and who, at the time he joined any such forces, was domiciled in Canada.
This man may have come here simply to enlist. This thing was done in the first world war and it is being done in the second, on account of the promises that were made by the government. Sometimes men were not domiciled in Canada before the war, but were given the opportunity to come here and take advantage of all the benefits that were being offered to Canadians. One example is the
4,000	Polish soldiers who will be given benefits that are being refused to Canadians who were in the army.
I cannot understand why men who have fought under different colours, not even British colours, should be placed ahead of our own men who have worn the Canadian
uniform. I mentioned not long ago that some benefits are being given to complete strangers. It is admitted that these men fought in the same cause against Germany and Japan; they may have fought quite well, but that is no reason for making Canada the dumping ground for all the nations of the world. I said that in one of the committee rooms adjacent to Westminster Hall. Why should Canada be the dumping ground for all the nations of the world? Why should we do more than any other nation for outsiders? It is a strange thing.
I think of those Canadian boys, big and small; I think of those young men full of hope who came here but who met with such poor success because every place was occupied, there were no more vacancies, they had been given to outsiders. They were told, "You Canadians go away; there is no room for you." That is the policy that has been sponsored by the civil service commission. When the member for Temiscouata presided over that committee he got all that information from the civil service commission, about men who had come from all over the world to take positions that rightly belonged to red-blooded Canadians.
I have no objection to a well-balanced immigration policy, but I do not think any immigrant should take the place of a Canadian. I do not think any outsider should take the place of a man who has the right to get all the benefits that this country may offer. When I say "Canadian" I want it to be understood that I do not mean only those who were born here; not at all. That is precisely the reason why I have never joined the Native Sons of Canada. I mean also those who may have been born somewhere else in the world but who have made Canada their country of adoption, their country of love, the country they want for themselves and for their children, the country in which they intend to establish themselves permanently. These things should not apply to the migratory birds who came here just to get some advantages, just to get rich quick and then return to their country of origin. We do not need those people; they are not desirable immigrants.

subtopic: CANADIAN SERVICE MEN IN ALLIED FORCES AND THEIR DEPENDENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I expect that the bill now before the house will prove uncontroversial, as the previous one did. If I may, for a moment or two, I should like to cover the reasons why I approve the introduction of this measure.
As I understand it, the bill is to make provision for the nationals of other countries who were allied with His Majesty and who joined the forces of the countries of their origin, being recruited in Canada with the permission and concurrence of the Canadian government, and-may I emphasize this-with the cooperation of the Department of National Defence. speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Right Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Acting Prime Minister): Mr. Speaker, if I may have the unanimous consent of the house I should like to make a brief statement on behalf of the Prime Minister.
When in London at a meeting of Prime Ministers in May last, the Prime Minister extended an invitation to the Right Honourable Viscount Addison, Secretary of State for Dominion Affairs and Leader of the House of Lords, to visit Canada as a guest of our government at a time convenient to him. I am pleased to inform the house that I have received from the Prime Minister word that Lord Addison will visit Canada during the parliamentary recess. It is expected that Lord Addison will reach Halifax early in September and that he will spend the month of September in Canada. Lord Addison will be accompanied by Lady Addison.
As hon. members are doubtless aware, Lord Addison is a leading British statesman of great experience. He assumed his present office on the formation of the Labour government a year ago and he has held high cabinet posts in various governments during the last thirty years. These include service as Minister of Munitions and as the first Minister of Health in Mr. Lloyd George's cabinet during and after the first world war and as Minister of Agriculture in 1930-1931. On his visit to Canada I am sure that he will receive a most-cordial welcome from the Canadian people.
At six o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Thursday, August 8, 1946
